newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo '97 wheat buy up seen below plan, analysts.
newsitem.headline: Yugo '97 wheat buy up seen below plan, analysts.

text.p: Yugoslavia will fail to buy up planned quantities of 1997 wheat crop from its farmers because of an unfavourable payment schedule, analysts said on Thursday.
The government plans to buy up to one million tonnes of the crop and has already purchased some 350,000 tonnes in advance and intends to buy another 600,000 after the harvest.
Analysts doubt farmers will sell all their crop immediately. Many will store it to sell later.

"It can be expected that the farmers sell only a minimum of their wheat crop just to get enough money to cover sowing costs," undersecretary in the federal Agriculture Ministry Milan Prostran told Reuters.
Official preliminary 1997 wheat forecasts stand at 2.8 million tonnes from some 800,000 hectares against 1.5 million from 583,000 ha harvested in 1996.
Annual needs are estimated between two and 2.4 million tonnes.
Recent heavy rainfall and hail damaged huge wheat areas in the country's granary Vojvodina and analysts said the crop could be a few percent below the official forecast.
Shortages last year pushed wheat prices up to 1.4 or even 1.7 dinars per kilo at some stages against the guaranteed price of 0.9 dinars for '96 crop.
Farmers who sold their wheat later earned more than those who sold to the state immediately after harvest, which will have an impact on the sales to the state this year, analysts said.

The Serbian government set the purchase price of this year's crop at 1.1 dinar per kilo, 40 percent of which would be paid in cash by the end of August. The second and third instalments of 30 percent each will be paid in forward wheat contracts issued by Serbia's Commodity Reserve Agency maturing at the end of September and end of October.
Wheat can also be exchanged for fuel, fertilisers, seeds and agricultural equipment.
Agricultural producers saw the purchase price as satisfactory but were not happy with delayed payments.
"The price is good and farmers are happy with it. But payouts are late. Farmers demand to be paid in time," said Milan Pavlovic of the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives of Serbia.
"The farmers must buy fertilisers, seeds, prepare for the next sowing. If the government wants them to invest in production they must get money on time," he said.
Analysts worried there would be a repeat of 1996 when the government had no money to pay farmers for their crops.

"Vojvodina farmers are still owed some 100 million dinars ($17.23 million) for the '96 crop. Final payment is set for end of October and that is too late as it is already time of sowing," said Ljiljana Vasic, head of the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives of Vojvodina.

"At least 50-60 percent should be paid in cash. Money received for wheat is this year's first payment for crops to farmers who need it for re-investment and to prepare their children for school," she said. -- Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 311 4254
